objectives: Explain the US Constitution, amendments, + Marbury-anchored judicial review.
Map federalism — commerce, necessary-and-proper, supremacy, state sovereignty.
Trace rights doctrine from Brown to Dobbs.

slides.title: The Constitution + judicial review
slides.body:
The **United States Constitution** (1787; ratified 1788; effective 1789) is the world's oldest continuously operating written constitution. Drafted in Philadelphia by 55 delegates (including Madison, Hamilton, Franklin, Washington, Wilson, Sherman); ratified after a fierce campaign in which **James Madison**, **Alexander Hamilton**, + **John Jay** wrote the 85 *Federalist Papers* (1787-88). Its central design: a **republican** federal government of **enumerated + limited powers**, balanced by **separation of powers** (Articles I, II, III: Congress, President, Judiciary) + **federalism** (Article IV + the Tenth Amendment reserving residual powers to the states).

**Structure**:
- **Article I** — Congress (House + Senate; bicameralism + presentment; enumerated powers §8; limits §9; state limits §10).
- **Article II** — President (electoral college; commander-in-chief; appointment + treaty powers with Senate; take-care clause; impeachment).
- **Article III** — Judiciary (one Supreme Court + such inferior courts as Congress establishes; cases + controversies; original + appellate jurisdiction; treason clause).
- **Article IV** — full faith + credit; privileges + immunities; new states; guarantee of republican government.
- **Article V** — amendment process (2/3 of both Houses + 3/4 of states; or convention + ratification — never used).
- **Article VI** — Supremacy Clause; oaths; no religious test.
- **Article VII** — ratification.

**Bill of Rights (1791)**: Amendments I-X, drafted by Madison from state ratifying-convention demands. I — speech, press, religion, assembly, petition. II — arms. III — quartering. IV — searches + seizures. V — grand jury, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, due process, takings. VI — speedy + public trial, jury, counsel, confrontation. VII — civil jury. VIII — bail + cruel/unusual. IX — non-enumerated rights. X — reserved powers.

**Reconstruction Amendments (1865-1870)**: XIII — abolition of slavery. XIV — citizenship, **Due Process**, **Equal Protection**, **Privileges or Immunities**, §5 enforcement power. XV — voting regardless of race. These rewired the federal-state balance after the Civil War + are the textual home of most modern rights doctrine.

**Other key amendments**: XVI — income tax (1913). XVII — direct election of senators (1913). XIX — women's suffrage (1920). XXII — two-term presidential limit (1951). XXIV — anti-poll-tax (1964). XXVI — 18-year-old vote (1971).

**Marbury v. Madison (1803)** — **Chief Justice John Marshall** for a unanimous Court. The most important constitutional decision in American history. Facts: outgoing Federalist administration commissioned William Marbury as a DC justice of the peace; commission undelivered; new Secretary of State James Madison refused to deliver. Marbury sued in the Supreme Court for a writ of mandamus under the Judiciary Act of 1789 §13. Marshall's brilliance: held Marbury had a right + a remedy, but the Court had no jurisdiction because **§13 of the Judiciary Act unconstitutionally expanded the Court's original jurisdiction** beyond what **Article III §2** allows. Thus the Court asserted **judicial review** — the power to declare congressional acts unconstitutional — while denying jurisdiction (so political backlash was muted). 'It is emphatically the province + duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.' Foundation of the American judicial system.

Related Marshall Court cornerstones:
- **Fletcher v. Peck (1810)** — first federal statute (state, this time) struck under Constitution.
- **Martin v. Hunter's Lessee (1816)** + **Cohens v. Virginia (1821)** — Supreme Court reviews state-court constitutional decisions.
- **McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)** — implied powers via the Necessary + Proper Clause; states cannot tax federal instrumentalities ('the power to tax involves the power to destroy').
- **Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)** — broad reading of the Commerce Clause; struck NY steamboat monopoly.

**Article III** confines federal courts to **cases + controversies** — no advisory opinions, ripeness, mootness, standing (injury + causation + redressability), political-question doctrine. These justiciability doctrines police the courts' constitutional role + remain heavily litigated.

slides.title: Federalism: powers, commerce, supremacy, sovereignty
slides.body:
**Federalism** — the vertical division of authority between the federal government + the states — is one of the Constitution's two structural innovations (the other is separation of powers).

**Enumerated federal powers** (Article I §8) include taxation, borrowing, regulation of commerce among the states + with foreign nations, naturalization, bankruptcy, coining money, post offices, patents + copyrights, federal courts inferior to the Supreme Court, piracy, declare war + raise armies + a navy, militia, district seat (DC), forts + arsenals — + the **Necessary + Proper Clause** at the end of §8.

**McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)** — Marshall: the **Necessary + Proper Clause** authorizes any 'appropriate' + 'plainly adapted' means to carry into execution an enumerated power. The Second Bank of the United States was within congressional power even though not enumerated; Maryland's tax on it was unconstitutional under the Supremacy Clause. 'Let the end be legitimate... + all means which are appropriate... + not prohibited... are constitutional.' Foundational for the modern administrative state.

**Commerce Clause** (Article I §8 cl. 3) — 'To regulate Commerce... among the several States.' Doctrinal arc:
- **Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)** — broad initial reading.
- **Lochner era** (1890s-1937) — narrow reading; courts struck progressive economic regulation under doctrines of dual federalism + substantive due process. **Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918)** invalidated federal child-labor regulation.
- **New Deal crisis + switch in time (1937)**: **West Coast Hotel v. Parrish** + **NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel** + **United States v. Darby (1941)** — Commerce Clause broadened; *Hammer* overruled.
- **Wickard v. Filburn (1942)** — aggregation principle; Farmer Filburn's home-grown wheat for personal consumption, in aggregate, affected interstate commerce; sustains expansive regulation.
- **Heart of Atlanta Motel (1964)** + **Katzenbach v. McClung (1964)** — sustained Title II of the Civil Rights Act under Commerce Clause; restaurants + hotels affected interstate commerce.
- **United States v. Lopez (1995)** — first reversal in 58 years; Gun-Free School Zones Act exceeded commerce power; not economic activity.
- **United States v. Morrison (2000)** — Violence Against Women Act civil remedy exceeded commerce power.
- **Gonzales v. Raich (2005)** — federal marijuana prohibition reached intrastate medical use under aggregation.
- **NFIB v. Sebelius (2012)** — **Roberts** held ACA individual mandate exceeded commerce + Necessary + Proper powers, but sustained under taxing power. Limited 'inactivity' regulation.

**Spending Clause + Conditions on Federal Funds**: **South Dakota v. Dole (1987)** — Congress can condition federal funds on state policy compliance (drinking-age tied to highway funds) if related + not coercive. **NFIB v. Sebelius** — ACA Medicaid expansion crossed the coercion line (a 'gun to the head' of states).

**Supremacy Clause** (Article VI cl. 2) — federal law (Constitution, statutes, treaties) is the supreme law of the land. **Preemption** doctrine: express, field, conflict (impossibility + obstacle). **Gibbons v. Ogden** + countless modern preemption cases.

**State sovereignty + Tenth Amendment + anti-commandeering**:
- **New York v. United States (1992)** — Congress cannot **commandeer** state legislatures (radioactive-waste take-title invalid).
- **Printz v. United States (1997)** — Scalia: cannot commandeer state executive officials (Brady Bill background checks).
- **Murphy v. NCAA (2018)** — anti-commandeering extends to negative commands; PASPA's prohibition on state legalization of sports betting invalid.

**Eleventh Amendment + sovereign immunity**: states are immune from suit in federal court by citizens; **Seminole Tribe (1996)** + **Alden v. Maine (1999)** entrenched + extended. **Ex parte Young (1908)** — suits against state officers for prospective injunctive relief permitted (judge-made workaround essential to constitutional litigation).

**Dormant Commerce Clause**: even without congressional action, states may not discriminate against or unduly burden interstate commerce. **Cooley v. Board of Wardens (1851)**; modern test in **Pike v. Bruce Church (1970)** + **Granholm v. Heald (2005)** + **National Pork Producers (2023)**.

Federalism today is a live battleground: marijuana legalization, sanctuary cities, immigration, abortion post-*Dobbs*, climate, election administration, AI regulation.

slides.title: Rights: due process, equal protection, speech, + landmark cases
slides.body:
**The Fourteenth Amendment (1868)** is the source of most modern constitutional rights against the states.

**Incorporation**: the Bill of Rights originally bound only the federal government (**Barron v. Baltimore**, 1833 — Marshall). The Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause was used by the **Lochner era** Court for substantive economic rights (1890s-1937); then by the **Warren Court** (1953-1969) to *incorporate* most Bill of Rights protections against the states via **selective incorporation** — **Mapp v. Ohio** (4th, 1961), **Gideon v. Wainwright** (6th counsel, 1963), **Pointer v. Texas** (6th confrontation, 1965), **Miranda v. Arizona** (5th, 1966), **Duncan v. Louisiana** (6th jury, 1968). **McDonald v. Chicago** (2010) — Second Amendment incorporated. **Timbs v. Indiana** (2019) — excessive-fines clause incorporated. Only a few clauses remain non-incorporated (grand jury, 7th civil jury, some others).

**Equal Protection Clause**: 'No State shall... deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws.' Tiered scrutiny:
- **Strict scrutiny** — race, national origin, alienage (federal): compelling interest + narrowly tailored. Used in *Brown*, *Loving*, *Korematsu* (notoriously upholding internment, repudiated *Trump v. Hawaii* 2018).
- **Intermediate scrutiny** — sex (*Craig v. Boren* 1976; *United States v. Virginia* 1996 — VMI all-male admissions invalid; Ginsburg majority): important interest + substantially related. Also non-marital children.
- **Rational basis** — economic, social welfare: legitimate interest + rationally related. Highly deferential. But **rational-basis-with-bite**: *Cleburne* (1985, mental disability), *Romer v. Evans* (1996, sexual orientation), *Lawrence v. Texas* (2003, sodomy).

**Brown v. Board of Education (1954)** — Warren Court unanimous (**Chief Justice Earl Warren**). 'Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.' Overruled *Plessy v. Ferguson* (1896). Foundation of modern equal-protection jurisprudence + the civil-rights movement. *Brown II* (1955) — desegregation 'with all deliberate speed.' Implementation litigation continued for decades (*Cooper v. Aaron* 1958; busing cases; *Milliken v. Bradley* 1974 limited interdistrict remedies).

**Loving v. Virginia (1967)** — Warren Court unanimous. Struck Virginia's anti-miscegenation law. Foundation for marriage cases (*Obergefell*).

**Substantive due process** — privacy + autonomy rights:
- **Griswold v. Connecticut (1965)** — **Justice Douglas**: 'penumbras' + 'emanations' of the Bill of Rights protect marital contraception privacy. Justice Goldberg concurrence relied on the 9th Amendment.
- **Eisenstadt v. Baird (1972)** — extended contraception privacy to unmarried.
- **Roe v. Wade (1973)** — Blackmun: trimester framework; abortion right within Fourteenth Amendment liberty. One of the most controversial cases in American history.
- **Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992)** — joint opinion of O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter: reaffirmed *Roe* essential holding but replaced trimester with undue-burden standard.
- **Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health (2022)** — **Justice Alito** for the majority: overruled *Roe* + *Casey*. 'The Constitution does not confer a right to abortion... Roe + Casey must be overruled.' Returned abortion to state legislative determination. Triggered nationwide statutory wave, ballot initiatives, presidential elections. Concurrence by **Justice Thomas** signaled potential reconsideration of *Griswold*, *Lawrence*, *Obergefell* — although the majority denied that implication.

**Sexual orientation + same-sex marriage**:
- **Bowers v. Hardwick (1986)** — sustained Georgia sodomy law.
- **Lawrence v. Texas (2003)** — Kennedy: overruled *Bowers*; struck Texas sodomy law on substantive due process.
- **United States v. Windsor (2013)** — Kennedy: struck DOMA §3.
- **Obergefell v. Hodges (2015)** — Kennedy: states must license + recognize same-sex marriages; fundamental right.
- **Bostock v. Clayton County (2020)** — Gorsuch: Title VII forbids employment discrimination on basis of sexual orientation + gender identity (statutory case but with constitutional resonance).

**First Amendment — speech, religion, press, assembly**:
- **Schenck v. United States (1919)** — Holmes: 'clear + present danger.' **Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969)** — imminent lawless action: the modern test.
- **New York Times v. Sullivan (1964)** — Brennan: public officials must prove **actual malice** (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard); foundation of modern press law.
- **Tinker v. Des Moines (1969)** — student speech (armbands).
- **Texas v. Johnson (1989)** — flag-burning protected.
- **Citizens United v. FEC (2010)** — Kennedy: corporate + union political-speech spending protected; reshaped campaign finance.
- **Reed v. Town of Gilbert (2015)** — content-based speech regulation triggers strict scrutiny.
- **NIFLA v. Becerra (2018)** + **303 Creative (2023)** — compelled-speech jurisprudence.

**Religion**: Free Exercise — **Employment Division v. Smith (1990)** (Scalia: neutral generally applicable laws OK); **Hosanna-Tabor (2012)**; **Fulton (2021)**; **Kennedy v. Bremerton (2022)** rewrote Establishment Clause replacing *Lemon* with history + tradition. Establishment Clause — *Engel v. Vitale* (1962), *Lemon v. Kurtzman* (1971, overruled by *Kennedy*), *Town of Greece* (2014), *American Legion* (2019).

**Voting + democracy**: *Baker v. Carr* (1962, justiciability of redistricting), *Reynolds v. Sims* (1964, one-person-one-vote), *Shelby County v. Holder* (2013, struck VRA §4(b) preclearance formula), *Rucho v. Common Cause* (2019, partisan gerrymandering non-justiciable), *Allen v. Milligan* (2023, racial gerrymandering).

Constitutional law is an evolving conversation among courts, legislatures, executives, advocates, scholars, + the public — the central arena of American political + moral argument.

question.question: Apply tiered equal-protection scrutiny to a hypothetical
question.goal: A state law forbids non-citizens from working as public-school teachers. Analyze under Equal Protection.

steps.prompt: What classification does the law use, + what scrutiny tier applies?

acceptedAnswers: Alienage classification by a state; generally strict scrutiny but a political-function exception applies (Foley v Connelie 1978; Ambach v Norwick 1979)

hints: State alienage classifications + the political-function exception.
steps.reveal: State alienage classifications normally trigger **strict scrutiny** (*Graham v. Richardson* 1971). But the Court carved a **political-function exception** — states may restrict participation in self-government to citizens at rational-basis. **Foley v. Connelie (1978)** sustained citizenship requirement for state troopers; **Ambach v. Norwick (1979)** sustained it for public-school teachers (citizenship goes to inculcation of civic values).

steps.prompt: Under the political-function exception, what test applies + is the law likely valid?

acceptedAnswers: Rational basis under the political-function exception (Ambach v Norwick); the law is likely sustained

steps.reveal: Under *Ambach*, the law is reviewed at **rational basis**. The state's interest in selecting teachers who embody + transmit American democratic values is legitimate; the citizenship classification is rationally related. The law is likely sustained — though some narrower variations could fail (e.g., applied to non-teachers, or to longtime LPRs with declared intent to naturalize).

steps.prompt: What if the law were federal rather than state? Different result?

acceptedAnswers: Federal alienage classifications get rational-basis review (Mathews v Diaz 1976) given congressional plenary power over immigration

steps.reveal: **Mathews v. Diaz (1976)** — federal alienage classifications get rational basis given Congress's plenary power over immigration + naturalization (Article I §8 cl. 4). So if Congress did this, it would face only rational basis even without the political-function exception.

steps.prompt: Could a plaintiff still prevail via a different constitutional theory?

acceptedAnswers: Possibly preemption — federal immigration law preempts state alienage classifications in some areas (e.g., Arizona v US 2012); plus Title VII national-origin claim; supremacy clause

steps.reveal: **Preemption** — state alienage rules may be preempted where they conflict with federal immigration policy (*Arizona v. United States* 2012; *Graham v. Richardson* 1971 also invoked preemption). **Title VII**'s national-origin protection (Civil Rights Act of 1964) may reach some discrimination though not pure citizenship requirements. **Anti-commandeering** doctrines could play a role in some immigration-cooperation contexts. The full analysis combines equal protection + preemption + statutory doctrines.

question.question: Why is **Marbury v. Madison (1803)** considered the foundation of American constitutional law?
options: **Marbury v. Madison (1803)** — Chief Justice John Marshall, unanimous Court — established **judicial review**: the power of the federal judiciary to declare acts of Congress unconstitutional. Marshall achieved this on facts uniquely favorable to the Court's institutional position: William Marbury had a *right* + a *remedy*, but §13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 — under which he sued — unconstitutionally expanded the Court's original jurisdiction beyond Article III §2's enumeration. The Court therefore denied jurisdiction *while asserting* the power to strike a federal statute — minimizing political backlash from the Jefferson administration. 'It is emphatically the province + duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.' Marbury operationalizes **constitutional supremacy** (Article VI) by making the judiciary its final enforcer, anchors **separation of powers**, + structures every subsequent constitutional case from *Brown* (1954) to *Dobbs* (2022). Without *Marbury* the Constitution would be a parchment promise enforced only by the political branches that it constrains.
question.explanation: Marbury established judicial review — federal courts' power to declare congressional acts unconstitutional. Marshall avoided backlash by denying jurisdiction while asserting the power. Anchors constitutional supremacy + separation of powers; foundation of every subsequent constitutional case.

slides.workedSolution: Marbury (1803, Marshall) established judicial review — courts can declare congressional acts unconstitutional. Marshall denied jurisdiction (avoiding political collision) while asserting the power. Anchors constitutional supremacy + separation of powers; structures all subsequent constitutional doctrine.

question.question: A state's new abortion law: post-Dobbs constitutional architecture
question.prompt: After **Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health (2022)**, State A enacts a six-week abortion ban with no rape/incest exception. (a) Identify the relevant federal-constitutional challenges available post-Dobbs (Equal Protection? Due Process? Right to Travel? Establishment Clause? Privileges or Immunities?). (b) State B enacts a 'shield law' protecting in-state providers who treat State A residents — analyze full-faith-+-credit, dormant Commerce Clause, + extraterritoriality issues. (c) If Congress passes a federal abortion-protection statute, identify constitutional sources of authority (Commerce Clause? §5 of the 14th? Spending Clause?) + how each might fare under recent doctrine (*Lopez*, *Morrison*, *NFIB*, *Boerne*). (d) Predict how state constitutions + state supreme courts (e.g., Kansas, Michigan, Ohio) reshape the legal landscape post-Dobbs even when federal protection is gone.

question.question: Article V supermajority — how many of the 50 states must ratify a proposed constitutional amendment to make it operative?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain the structural architecture of American constitutional law: enumeration, judicial review, separation of powers, federalism, + rights.
question.rubric: Mentions: the **US Constitution** establishes a federal government of **enumerated + limited powers** (Article I §8) balanced by **separation of powers** (Articles I-III: Congress, President, Judiciary) + **federalism** (Article IV + the 10th Amendment). **Marbury v. Madison (1803, Marshall)** + **McCulloch (1819)** + **Gibbons (1824)** put judicial review + broad federal power in place. The **Reconstruction Amendments** (XIII-XV) rewired the federal-state balance + are textually responsible for most modern rights doctrine via **incorporation** + the **Equal Protection Clause** + **Due Process Clause**. Landmarks include **Brown** (1954, Warren), **Loving** (1967), **Griswold** (1965), **Roe** (1973), **Obergefell** (2015), **Dobbs** (2022). Speech: **Sullivan** (1964, Brennan), **Brandenburg** (1969), **Citizens United** (2010). The system continues to evolve through new doctrines + new constitutional moments. Concludes: constitutional law is the live ongoing operating system of American government.
